summary: Defines the Session Description Protocol, a text format for describing multimedia sessions for announcement, invitation and other forms of session initiation. It is widely used with SIP and RTP. It was standards-track and has been replaced by RFC 8866.

plainLanguage.summary: SDP is a text format for describing a multimedia session, including its media, timing and transport addresses. Other protocols carry the description to the participants.

questions: what is the o= line in sdp
subtitle: A text format that describes the media, timing and addresses for a session.

tldr.problem: People need a consistent way to describe media, timing and transport details when announcing or starting multimedia sessions.
tldr.mechanism: SDP uses ordered text lines, with session-level information followed by optional media-level descriptions. It can be carried by other protocols and uses attributes as its main extension mechanism.
tldr.outcome: SDP describes a session but does not transport it or negotiate media formats. RFC 4566 has been obsoleted by RFC 8866.

today: RFC 4566 is a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 2327 and RFC 3266. It has itself been obsoleted by RFC 8866.

sections.title: What a Session Description Provides
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) gives a standard format for describing multimedia sessions, including calls, conferences and streaming media. The description can be delivered by protocols such as SIP, RTSP, email or HTTP.

SDP conveys enough information to discover and participate in a session, including its name, active times, media and the addresses and ports needed to receive the media. It does not provide a transport protocol or negotiate media encodings.
sections.plainLanguage: SDP describes a session and the information needed to join it. A separate protocol carries that description to other participants.

sections.title: Lines and Session Structure
sections.content:
An SDP description is text made of lines in the form type=value. Each line's type is one case-sensitive character, and whitespace is not allowed beside the equals sign. Lines must follow a fixed order.

The session-level section begins with v=. It is followed by zero or more media-level sections, each beginning with m=. Session-level connection data and attributes apply to all media unless a media section supplies an override.
sections.plainLanguage: An SDP description is a list of short, labeled lines in a required order. It starts with details for the whole session, then can give separate details for each media stream.

sections.title: Session and Media Fields
sections.content:
Required session fields identify the SDP version, origin and session name, and give at least one time description. Other lines can provide connection addresses, bandwidth, a URI, contact information, encryption-key data or attributes.

Each media section gives a media name, port, transport protocol and one or more formats. An attribute can give additional information about a session or media stream. Receivers ignore attributes they do not understand, while an unknown line type makes the whole description unusable to that parser.
sections.plainLanguage: The session lines identify the session and its timing. Each media block says what kind of stream it is and how a receiver can receive it.

sections.title: Trust and Security
sections.content:
A session description cannot be trusted unless it arrives through an authenticated transport from a trusted source. A false description could name an unexpected destination or change media parameters.

The RFC says a parser must not start software other than configured multimedia software, and a description must not start an interactive session without the user's prior authorization. It also warns that the k= field carries encryption keys in cleartext and must not be used for key material unless the channel is private and authenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: A session description can direct software to connect to an address, so the receiver needs to consider whether its source is trusted. The RFC warns against sending keys in a description carried over an unprotected channel.
